extracted.intended_audience: administrative-law practitioners, judges, regulators, and litigants involved in agency rulemaking/NEPA disputes
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for when and how courts may review or impose procedures on agency rulemaking (interaction of APA §553, NEPA, and judicial deference), including adequacy of record, scope of alternatives, threshold for intervenor comments, and the role of technical advisory reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency procedural discretion/deference
rubrics_metrics.description: Absent constitutional constraints or extremely compelling circumstances, administrative agencies 'should be free to fashion their own rules of procedure and to pursue methods of inquiry' to discharge their duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should not impose their own conception of 'best' procedures on agencies; agencies' procedural choices are presumptively within their discretion. See FCC v. Schreiber and related authority quoted in text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on judicial imposition of extra procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may not routinely require more than the procedural minima set by statute (e.g., 5 U.S.C. § 553) simply because an issue is complex or of great public import.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative history indicates §553 reflects minimum requirements; agencies may in addition confer with committees, consult organizations, hold informal hearings, etc., as practicality and public interest govern. Judicially imposing extra procedures would create unpredictability and disrupt the statutory scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remand vs. judicial dictation of methods
rubrics_metrics.description: When additional evidence is needed, a reviewing court should remand to the agency rather than dictate the methods, procedures, and time dimension of the needed inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A court 'may not . . . proceed by dictating to the agency the methods, procedures, and time dimension of the needed inquiry' because that risks intruding into a domain reserved for agencies (quoting Transcontinental Gas Pipe Line Corp. and SEC v. Chenery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Review of agency procedural choices based on information available at decision time
rubrics_metrics.description: A court should evaluate an agency's choice of procedures on the basis of the record actually produced and the information available to the agency when it structured the proceedings, not with hindsight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monday-morning quarterbacking (judging by information only available later) is improper and encourages agencies to adopt adjudicatory procedures in all proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of the record tied to statutory mandate, not procedural form
rubrics_metrics.description: The adequacy of the administrative 'record' for rulemaking turns on whether the agency has followed the statutory mandate (APA or other statutes), not on whether formal adjudicatory devices were used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informal rulemaking need not be based solely on hearing transcripts; holding agencies to an adjudicatory-record standard for every rule would force adjudicatory hearings for all rulemakings and defeat informal rulemaking benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: NEPA imposes only its plain-language procedural requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: NEPA does not by implication repeal or expand other statutes' procedures; its procedural obligations are only those stated in the Act's plain language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NEPA cannot serve as a basis for substantially revising the procedural specifications of the APA; courts should look to NEPA's explicit text for procedural duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of alternatives in an EIS limited by feasibility and state of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency's required discussion of 'alternatives' in an EIS is bounded by feasibility and what can be meaningfully analyzed given available knowledge at the time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NEPA was not meant to require detailed discussion of remote, speculative alternatives whose effects cannot be readily ascertained or would require fundamental changes in other statutes or policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal/evolving nature of alternatives obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept of what alternatives must be considered evolves as alternatives become better known and understood; agencies are judged by the information available when they acted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory developments (e.g., guidelines introduced only after draft/final statements) may render certain alternatives irrelevant or not reasonably foreseeable at the time of the agency's action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intervenor comment materiality/threshold requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments must be significant enough to pass a threshold of materiality before lack of agency response becomes a basis for review; a comment must show why an alleged mistake could be significant to the results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere assertion that a mistake was made is insufficient; intervenors must structure participation so it is meaningful and alerts the agency to specific positions and contentions (quoting Portland Cement Assn. v. Ruckelshaus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commission/agency threshold test for contentions
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency may apply a threshold test for the presentation of contentions that is not equivalent to a civil prima facie burden but requires a showing 'sufficient to require reasonable minds to inquire further.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a threshold is within agency discretion and is not an unduly heavy burden in the rulemaking/administrative setting (the Commission's explicit language quoted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on courts substituting their judgment for agency environmental determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should not substitute their judgment for that of the agency on the environmental consequences of agency actions; judicial review is limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neither statute nor legislative history contemplates courts substituting their judgment for agencies on environmental consequences (citing Kleppe v. Sierra Club).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on judicial ordering of clarification of technical advisory reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts lack authority to require technical advisory committees (e.g., ACRS) to rewrite or elaborate reports into layman's terms or to order agencies to return reports for such clarification absent statutory authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The principal function of such reports is to provide technical advice to the agency; publication to the public is subsidiary. Reports may refer to previous reports on file; the absence of lay explanations does not automatically invalidate agency action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for setting aside administrative decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative decisions should be set aside only for substantial procedural or substantive reasons as mandated by statute (e.g., arbitrary, capricious, or not supported by the administrative record), not merely because a court disagrees with the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single alleged oversight on a peripheral issue, especially urged by parties who did not cooperatively present the issue below, should not serve as grounds for overturning a properly made decision after exhaustive proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency ability to supplement minima when practical
rubrics_metrics.description: While §553 establishes minimum public rulemaking procedures, agencies may in addition confer with industry advisory committees, consult organizations, hold informal hearings, and the like, guided by practicality and public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative history contemplates such supplemental procedures where useful or protective to the public, especially in matters of great import.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of historical/regulatory context in judging agency tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should account for the historical setting and evolving regulatory landscape when assessing agency procedural tests (e.g., 'threshold test' for energy-conservation contentions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism of agency procedural choices that ignores when the agency acted and what was known at the time misconceives both statutory responsibility and administrative process.
